statement.p: An experiment to measure the toxicity of formaldehyde yielded the data in the table below. The values show the percent, P=f(t,c), of rats surviving an exposure to formaldehyde at a concentration of c (in parts per million, ppm) after t months.

p.em: (Be sure that you can give the practical meaning of these two values in terms of formaldehyde toxicity.)

static.solution:
f(16,2) = 99.
(a) Thus, to estimate f_t(16,2), we can take f_t(16,2) \approx \frac{f(16+2,2) - f(16-2,2)}{4} = \frac{98 - 100}{4} = -0.5. Alternately, we could take either of the two one-sided difference quotients, f_t(16,2) \approx \frac{f(16+2,2) - f(16,2)}{2} = -0.5 or f_t(16,2) \approx \frac{f(16,2) - f(16-2,2)}{2} = -0.5. In each case, the units of f_t are percent per month. This says 16 months after rats are exposed to a formaldehyde concentration of 2 ppm, the percent of rats surviving is decreasing at a rate of about -0.5 per month. In other words, during the 16 month, around an additional -0.5 percent of the rats will die.
(b) Proceeding similarly to find f_c(16,2), we have f_c(16,2) \approx \frac{f(16,2+2) - f(16,2-2)}{4} = \frac{95 - 100}{4} = -0.833333, or, with one-sided difference quotients, f_c(16,2) \approx \frac{f(16,2+2) - f(16,2)}{2} = -1 or f_c(16,2) \approx \frac{f(16,2) - f(16,2-2)}{2} = -0.5. These indicate that if the original concentration increases from 2 by 1 ppm, the percent surviving after 16 months decreases by about 0.83.
